error.noPluginDir: This panel could not locate its own plugin directory, so the backend cannot be run.
error.pamNotRegistered: Register the key with PAM first — there is nothing in %1 to match against.
confirm.disableApplet:
Disable the %1 applet over USB?

Anything relying on it stops working until you turn it back on.
error.accountIncomplete: An account needs at least a name and the secret the provider showed you.
busy.readingCode: Reading a code for %1 — touch the key if it blinks
confirm.deleteAccount:
Delete %1 from the key?

The secret is destroyed. Re-adding it needs the original from the provider.
error.noGpgPublic: gpg does not have the public half of this key yet. Import it, or run `gpg --card-edit` then `fetch`.
header.toolingMissing: Supporting packages are missing — open Setup.
header.noKey: No key detected. Plug one in, then refresh.
device.toolsMissingTitle: The YubiKey tools are not installed yet
device.toolsMissingBody: This page reads the key through ykman, which is not on this machine yet. The Setup tab installs it along with everything else the other pages need.
device.noKeyBody: Plug the key in and press Refresh. If it is already in, the key may have an applet disabled, or the smartcard daemon may not be running — Setup can tell you which.
applets.title: Applets
applets.intro: A YubiKey is several independent devices sharing one body. Switching one off over USB hides it from this machine entirely — useful for narrowing what a key exposes, and an easy way to lose access to something if you forget you did it.
applet.fido2: Passkeys, WebAuthn security keys, SSH -sk keys, LUKS unlock
applet.u2f: The older second-factor protocol, still used by some sites
applet.oath: TOTP codes for Gmail, Outlook, AWS — the Accounts tab
applet.piv: Smartcard certificates, usable for SSH over PKCS#11
applet.openpgp: GPG keys on the card, and gpg-agent as an SSH agent
applet.otp: Yubico OTP and the static-password slots
pins.title: PINs
pins.intro: Each applet keeps its own PIN and its own retry counter. Run out of retries and the applet locks; on FIDO2 that means a factory reset and re-registering everywhere. These open a terminal, because a PIN prompt belongs in one.
pin.fido2SetDesc: Required by passkeys and by SSH keys made with verify-required.
pin.fido2UnsetDesc: Not set yet. Passkeys and verify-required SSH keys need one.
pin.pivDefault: Still on the factory PIN (123456) — anyone with the key in hand can use the slots. Change it before putting anything in one.
pin.pivStaleBoth: The PIV PUK and the management key are still set to the factory default. Change them from a terminal with `omarchy-yubikey pin piv-puk` and `omarchy-yubikey pin piv-mgmt` before the PIV applet holds anything worth guarding.
pin.pivStalePuk: The PIV PUK is still set to the factory default. Change it from a terminal with `omarchy-yubikey pin piv-puk` before the PIV applet holds anything worth guarding.
pin.pivStaleMgmt: The PIV management key is still set to the factory default. Change it from a terminal with `omarchy-yubikey pin piv-mgmt` before the PIV applet holds anything worth guarding.
pin.openpgpDesc: Guards the GPG keys on the card. Default is 123456, with 12345678 as the admin PIN.
reset.title: Reset an applet
reset.intro: Each of these wipes one applet back to factory state and cannot be undone. The terminal asks you to type the applet name before anything happens.
reset.fido2.note: Drops every passkey and site registration
reset.piv.note: Destroys all slot keypairs and certificates
reset.openpgp.note: Destroys the GPG keys on the card
pam.title: Logging into this machine
pam.intro: PAM is the stack every password prompt on this machine goes through. Registering writes this key's public credential to %1; each switch below then adds one `sufficient` line to that prompt's stack, so a touch satisfies it and your password still works if the key is not around.
pam.registerAnotherDesc: Adds a second key to the same file — worth doing before you rely on the first one.
pam.registerDesc: Opens a terminal, asks for a touch, and writes the credential. Nothing below works until this is done.
pam.sudoDesc: Touch the key instead of typing your password at a sudo prompt.
pam.polkitDesc: The dialog Omarchy raises when an app needs root. The file is created if it does not exist.
pam.loginDesc: The text logins on tty2–tty6. The graphical greeter has its own stack and is not covered.
pam.lockDesc: Omarchy's lock screen. Note the trade: the stack asks for a touch before it checks the password, so unlocking without the key means waiting that prompt out first.
ssh.intro: Three unrelated ways to put an SSH identity on the key, and a key can hold all three. FIDO2 is the simple one: OpenSSH speaks it directly, with no agent and no daemon.
ssh.plugIn: Plug the key in to see what it holds.
ssh.noCardKey: No PIV or OpenPGP SSH key on the key.
ssh.pivUnreadable: The PIV applet could not be read — it needs pcscd and a PKCS#11 module.
ssh.residentNote: FIDO2 resident keys need the PIN to list, so they open in a terminal. Non-resident keys are not stored on the key at all.
ssh.listResidentDesc: Asks for the FIDO2 PIN in a terminal and shows the SSH credentials stored on the key, separately from website passkeys.
ssh.newResidentDesc: ed25519-sk stored on the key itself, protected by the FIDO2 PIN and a touch. Because it is resident, you can pull it back onto a new machine with nothing but the key.
ssh.newPlainDesc: Same touch requirement, but the handle lives only in ~/.ssh — lose the file and the key cannot recover it. Use this where a PIN prompt on every connection would be in the way.
ssh.recover: Recover resident keys from the key
ssh.recoverDesc: Writes the key handles for every resident credential back into ~/.ssh. This is what you run on a machine that has never seen this YubiKey.
ssh.piv: Use the PIV applet over PKCS#11
ssh.pivDesc: Points OpenSSH at %1 so a keypair in a PIV slot can authenticate. Needs pcscd running.
ssh.noModule: No PKCS#11 module is installed yet — Setup adds one.
ssh.gpg: Use gpg-agent as the SSH agent
ssh.gpgDesc: Exposes an OpenPGP authentication subkey on the card as an SSH identity. Takes effect after logging out and back in, since it sets SSH_AUTH_SOCK for the session.
luks.title: Disk encryption
luks.enroll: Unlock this disk with the key at boot
luks.desc: Enrolls the key as a FIDO2 unlock method for %1. Your passphrase stays valid and remains the only way in if the key is lost — keep it.
forget.title: Undo everything on this page
forget.desc: Removes every registered credential and takes pam_u2f back out of all four stacks. SSH keys and disk enrollments are left alone — those are removed where they were made.
accounts.title: Signing into your accounts
accounts.intro:
There are two ways an account can use this key, and most providers offer both.

As a security key or passkey, the registration happens in the browser on the provider's own page — no desktop can do it for you, so the list further down goes straight to the right settings page for each one.

As an authenticator, the provider shows you a secret and the key stores it. That part lives here: codes are generated from the key itself, so they survive a reinstall and never sit in a phone app.
oath.scan: Scan the QR code off the screen
oath.scanDesc: Drag a box around the QR code the provider is showing and the account is added from it. Far less error-prone than copying a base32 secret by hand.
oath.typeIt: Or type it in — providers always offer the secret as text behind a “can't scan the code?” link.
oath.touch: Require a touch for this account
oath.touchDesc: Reading a code then needs the key physically touched. Malware on this machine cannot pull codes in the background.
oath.locked: The OATH applet is password protected. Unlock it with `ykman oath access` in a terminal, then refresh.
oath.pick: Pick one to put its current code on the clipboard — it is cleared after one paste. Click ✕ to remove an account.
oath.deleteTip: Delete this account from the key
prov.title: Register as a security key
prov.intro: These open the page where each provider adds a security key or passkey. Have the key plugged in first — the browser asks for a touch partway through.
provider.google: Add under Passkeys and security keys. Works as a passkey or as a plain security key.
provider.microsoft: Security info > Add sign-in method > Security key. Hotmail and Outlook.com share this page.
provider.aws: Security credentials > Multi-factor authentication > Passkey or security key.
provider.github: Two-factor authentication > Security keys. Also where SSH keys are added.
setup.allInstalled: Everything this plugin needs is installed
setup.intro: None of these ship with Omarchy. Each one backs a specific page here, so a missing package shows up as a page that cannot do its job rather than an error.
setup.installDesc: Opens a terminal, installs the packages through omarchy-pkg-add, and enables pcscd.socket. You will be asked for your password.
dep.yubikey-manager: Read the key, toggle applets, manage PINs and TOTP accounts
dep.libfido2: Talk to the FIDO2 applet (SSH security keys, LUKS)
dep.pam-u2f: Register the key with PAM for sudo, polkit, login, and lock
dep.pcsclite: Smartcard daemon required by the PIV and OpenPGP applets
dep.yubico-piv-tool: Manage PIV certificates used for SSH and S/MIME
dep.opensc: PKCS#11 provider that lets OpenSSH use a PIV slot
dep.gnupg: OpenPGP applet, and gpg-agent as an SSH agent
dep.yubikey-personalization: Configure the OTP slots (Yubico OTP, static password)
setup.pcscdOn: pcscd.socket is active. The PIV and OpenPGP applets are reachable.
setup.pcscdOff: pcscd.socket is not active. The PIV and OpenPGP applets will not answer until it is — the install above enables it.
setup.terminalDesc: Everything this panel does is a subcommand of the script it ships with. `omarchy-yubikey doctor` prints the whole picture, and `omarchy-yubikey --help` lists the rest.
wiz.title: Security wizard
wiz.intro: Runs a checklist against this key and this machine, then walks you through what is left, one step at a time. Essentials close the holes every key ships with; the rest is worth doing once you rely on the key.
wiz.allDoneBody: Every step is done or skipped. Run the checklist again after changing anything on the key, or pick a step below to revisit it.
wiz.blocked.pam: Register the key with this machine first.
wiz.terminalNote: Opens a terminal. The checklist runs again on its own once it closes.
wiz.tools.why: ykman, libfido2, pam-u2f and pcscd are how every other step talks to the key. Without them the checklist cannot even read it.
wiz.key.why: The remaining checks read the key itself. If it is plugged in and still not seen, an applet may be switched off over USB.
wiz.fidoPin.why: Without a PIN, anyone holding the key can use its passkeys and resident SSH keys with a single touch. The key checks the PIN itself, and eight wrong guesses lock the applet.
wiz.fidoPin.warn: Only %1 tries left. One correct PIN entry resets the counter; reaching zero means a FIDO2 reset.
wiz.pivPin.why: Every YubiKey ships with PIV PIN 123456. Anything stored in a PIV slot later — an SSH key, a certificate — is only as private as that PIN.
wiz.pivPuk.why: The PUK unblocks a locked PIN. Left at 12345678, it lets anyone reset your PIN to one of their choosing.
wiz.pivMgmt.why: The management key authorizes writing to PIV slots, and the default one is public. This replaces it with a random key stored on the YubiKey itself, protected by your PIV PIN and a touch — you never need to remember it.
wiz.sshConfig.why: ~/.ssh/config tells OpenSSH to use the PIV applet, but no PIV slot holds an SSH key. Every connection then asks for the PIV PIN and tries the attestation key, which cannot sign — failed attempts that still count against the server's limit.
wiz.sshConfig.warn: PKCS11Provider is on, but the PIV slots are empty
wiz.sshConfig.ok: PKCS11Provider is on and a PIV key is present
wiz.pam: Register the key with this machine
wiz.pam.why: Lets sudo, polkit and the lock screen accept a touch. Your password keeps working; the key is an extra way in, not a replacement.
wiz.backup.why: A single key is a single point of failure. Register a second YubiKey everywhere you register this one — here, on GitHub, Google and the rest — and keep it somewhere safe. Plug the spare in before continuing.
wiz.sshKey.why: An ed25519-sk key whose private half never leaves the YubiKey. Protected by the FIDO2 PIN and a touch, and recoverable on a new machine with nothing but the key. Add the public key to GitHub afterwards.
wiz.sudo.why: A touch instead of typing your password at sudo prompts. The typed password is still accepted.
wiz.otp: Turn off Yubico OTP if you don't use it
wiz.otp.why: Brushing against the key types a long one-time password into whatever window has focus — chat boxes included. Few services still use Yubico OTP; switch it off unless one of yours does. It can be turned back on from the Device tab.
wiz.luks: Unlock the disk with the key
wiz.luks.why: Enrolls the key as a FIDO2 unlock method for %1. The passphrase stays valid — keep it, it is the way in if the key is lost.
